articles.headline: Miklós Seszták: Nuclear energy is indispensable for Hungary’s energy security

sentences.text: Strengthening the security of Hungary’s domestic energy supply is one of the most important tasks, and this cannot be achieved without nuclear power, said Miklós Seszták, nominee for Minister of National Development, at his hearing before Parliament’s Committee on Sustainable Development on Tuesday.

Referring to tensions between Ukraine and Russia, the minister-designate also stressed that dependence on gas is an issue that must be addressed, and that Hungary must be prepared for unexpected external events beyond its control.

In this context, he highlighted the need to continue the South Stream gas pipeline project, to enable bidirectional gas flows at the Hungarian–Croatian border, and to modernize and expand capacity on the Hungarian–Romanian section.
Seszták recalled that the already adopted National Energy Strategy and National Climate Change Strategy define the direction of the government and the ministry.
Maintaining the “nuclear–coal–renewables” energy mix outlined in the energy strategy is clearly justified and should not be altered, he emphasized.

With regard to renewable energy sources, he noted that Hungary committed to increasing the share of energy from renewables to 14.65% by 2020, exceeding the European Union’s required 13%, and that by 2012 the country had already reached the 9.6% target originally set for 2013.
“This is the right direction, but it must be made more efficient with appropriate regulatory instruments,” the minister-designate stated.

At his hearing before Parliament’s Committee on Enterprise Development on the same day, Seszták also pointed out that ensuring affordable—and, where possible, increasingly cheaper—energy is a key issue not only for households but also for industry.
According to him, this will be one of the major tasks of the next governmental cycle, although it is still too early to specify the extent of possible measures.

Seszták emphasized the importance of creating an economic and legal environment that supports business expansion and job creation, noting that promoting enterprise development is a key responsibility of the Ministry of National Development.
He also stated that in the future special attention will be given to simplifying and reducing administrative burdens on businesses.

Speaking about the principles of state asset management at hearings before the Committee on Sustainable Development, the Committee on Enterprise Development, as well as the Budgetary and Economic Committees, Seszták highlighted a key principle: “if public assets are sold, they should be used to create public assets.”
He added that during the previous government cycle, the Hungarian state had succeeded in strengthening its presence in strategic companies.
As examples, he mentioned the acquisition of a stake in MOL, the purchase of shares in Rába and the gas business of E.ON, as well as the reacquisition of Antenna Hungária.
These acquisitions, he argued, play an important role in protecting and continuing the policy of reducing household utility costs.
Regarding future plans, he referred to ongoing negotiations on the acquisition of the Budapest Sewage Works.

On public transport, he noted that the structural modernization of the MÁV Group has had a positive impact from a budgetary perspective, as the companies within the group closed the 2013 financial year with a profit, and following the restructuring, less budgetary support is required for their operation.
He added that efforts to improve the efficiency of MÁV’s operations must continue.
At all four committee hearings, the minister-designate denied having any interests in offshore companies.
He stated that he had worked as a lawyer for twenty years and, in that capacity, had been in contact with many business entities.
However, providing legal services to a company does not make him responsible for its activities, he said.

Parliament’s Committee on Sustainable Development supported Seszták’s appointment as Minister of National Development with 7 votes in favor and 3 against; the Committee on Enterprise Development with 6 in favor and 4 against; the Budgetary Committee with 10 in favor and 3 against; and the Economic Committee with 9 in favor, 3 against, and 1 abstention.
The Information Office should remain within the central structure of government

articles.headline: The Information Office should remain within the central structure of government

sentences.text: In the future, the work of the Information Office (IH) will place particular emphasis on economic and energy security.
As he explained, all threats to the Hungarian economy must be countered, and confidence in Hungary’s economy, as well as in the government securities and bond markets, must be maintained.
He added that the competitiveness of the Hungarian economy largely depends on energy prices.
The government aims to build an economic structure based on low-cost energy, within which, alongside affordable energy, the country’s energy independence must also be strengthened.
The minister-designate emphasized that, in order to ensure the country’s energy security and independence, special attention will be paid to Russia and Ukraine.
At the same time, he stated that the Paks investment agreement concluded with Russia does not pose a national security risk.
As he noted, the dependency risk associated with nuclear power plants lies in the origin of the fuel.
Paks II, however, will be a nuclear power plant capable of operating with fuel supplied from any source.
Paks power plant: the Hungarian government can convince the European Commission

articles.headline: Paks power plant: the Hungarian government can convince the European Commission

sentences.text: According to János Lázár, Minister-designate heading the Prime Minister’s Office, scientific publications demonstrate that it is worthwhile for Hungary to expand the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, and the government will be able to convince the European Commission of this.
Lázár made these remarks on Wednesday at a hearing before Parliament’s Committee on European Affairs, responding to a question from István Józsa (MSZP).

He noted that the expansion will be overseen by a government commissioner, and that, as part of consultations with the European Union, a “constructive, positive” technical meeting had taken place on Tuesday.

Based on this, the Hungarian government must clarify at least three issues before the European Commission: whether Hungary had the right to conclude an international agreement with Russia; whether the investment complies with EU rules on state aid; and how the independence of fuel procurement will be ensured—namely, whether fuel for the plant can be sourced from any supplier.

The pro-government politician described it as an irrefutable fact, supported by working groups of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (MTA), that the construction of Paks II is beneficial both for Hungary and for Europe.
He added that the government will be able to convince the European Commission of this.
“We will present the figures demonstrating the return on the investment and its role in guaranteeing low-cost energy within Hungary’s energy policy,” Lázár said.
He also warned that Hungary could lose its competitiveness in the near future if its industry and agriculture do not have access to affordable energy.

He further noted that nuclear energy will only be able to cover 50 percent of Hungary’s domestic energy demand, with the remaining demand to be met through imports and the development of renewable energy sources.
The Hungarian state will remain the sole owner of the Paks power plant

articles.headline: The Hungarian state will remain the sole owner of the Paks power plant

sentences.text: The Hungarian state will remain the exclusive owner of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant even after its expansion; therefore, decisions on the price of the electricity produced will remain exclusively in Hungarian hands, said Minister for National Economy Mihály Varga on Wednesday during the parliamentary debate on the loan agreement between the Hungarian and Russian governments.

According to his presentation, the Russian side will provide Hungary with a €10 billion credit line, covering 80 percent of the construction costs, while the remaining share will be financed by the Hungarian state from its own resources.
He noted that the loan is granted on terms more favorable than market conditions, with a maturity of 30 years.
Principal repayment will begin only after the plant becomes operational.
The interest rate will be 3.95 percent for the first eleven years of the loan period, after which it will gradually increase in seven-year intervals.

The minister drew attention to two key financial aspects of the loan: first, that it is consistent with the budget’s financing capacity and complies with the constitutional debt rule; and second, that it is not a commercial loan, meaning that its costs will not be incorporated into the price of electricity produced at Paks.
Varga described maintaining energy prices at a competitive level as a primary objective, which, in his view, is not possible without the expansion of Paks.
He also noted that the currently operating units are approaching the end of their service life and will be replaced by units equipped with the most modern technology.
In his view, all this will significantly improve the security of domestic electricity supply and reduce dependence on gas.
It will provide long-term security, he added, as the plant is designed for a lifespan of sixty years.
He also referred to the economic stimulus effect of the investment, stating that it will create approximately 10,000 new jobs and increase GDP by 1 percent.
He recalled that 40 percent of the investment would be allocated to domestic companies, generating at least €4 billion in revenue for them and potentially contributing €1 billion to the state budget.
The declining debt trajectory will be maintained during the expansion of Paks

articles.headline: The declining debt trajectory will be maintained during the expansion of Paks

sentences.text: The declining trajectory of public debt will be maintained even during the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, said Gábor Orbán, State Secretary for Taxation and Financial Affairs at the Ministry for National Economy (NGM), on Wednesday in Budapest at a meeting of Parliament’s Budgetary Committee.
The committee discussed the bill on promulgating the agreement with the Russian government concerning the disbursement of a state loan to finance the Paks expansion.
In response to a question from Erzsébet Schmuck (LMP), Vice-Chair of the committee, Gábor Orbán stated that the bill complies with the debt rule laid down in the Fundamental Law.

He added that, according to the calculations of the Ministry for National Economy, the costs associated with the Paks expansion—financed through the available credit facility—will arise at such a pace that the declining debt trajectory can be maintained alongside it.

In his remarks, Lajos Szűcs (Fidesz), another Vice-Chair of the committee, emphasized that the Paks expansion is an investment that increases Hungary’s assets, and thus “the growth in assets and the increase in public debt will create a state of equilibrium.” He argued that the Paks project cannot be compared to the loan taken by the Bajnai government from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the European Union, as that borrowing did not result in an increase in national assets.

The committee decided—with 9 votes in favor from governing party representatives and 3 against from opposition members—that the bill complies with procedural rules, and unanimously approved that the committee chair submit the bill to Parliament.
Parliament approves the Russian–Hungarian loan agreement

articles.headline: Parliament approves the Russian–Hungarian loan agreement

sentences.text: On Monday, Parliament approved the Russian–Hungarian loan agreement necessary to finance the development of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

The bill submitted by Minister for National Economy Mihály Varga—which includes the text of the agreement in both Hungarian and Russian—was adopted by the National Assembly with 110 votes in favor, 29 against, and 19 abstentions.
Members of Fidesz–KDNP voted in favor, while MSZP, LMP, and independent representatives opposed the proposal, and Jobbik abstained.
Following the vote, Bernadett Szél (LMP) handed a T-shirt bearing a protest message against the Paks expansion to Mihály Varga.

Under the loan agreement, the Russian side will provide Hungary with up to €10 billion in state credit to finance the planning, construction, commissioning, services, and procurement of equipment necessary for Units 5 and 6 of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.
The credit facility will cover 80 percent of construction and commissioning costs, with the remaining share to be financed by the Hungarian state from its own resources.
The Russian and Hungarian parties will agree—six months prior to each fiscal year—on the amount of the loan to be used in the upcoming budgetary period.
Amounts not drawn down relative to the pre-submitted plan will incur an availability fee charged by the Russian state.
The loan is to be utilized between 2014 and 2025, and the Hungarian side will repay it over a period of 21 years.
The first repayment installment will fall due on the March 15 or September 15 closest to the commissioning of Units 5 and 6 of the Paks plant, but no later than March 15, 2026.
Repayment will be structured as follows: 25 percent of the utilized loan amount during the first seven years, 35 percent during the next seven years, and 40 percent during the final seven years.
Hungary has the right to prepay any amount free of charge, provided that the Russian side is notified 90 days in advance.
Interest on the outstanding loan balance will be 3.95 percent annually from 2014 until the March 15 or September 15 closest to the commissioning of Units 5 and 6, but no later than March 15, 2026.
Thereafter, the interest rate will be 4.50 percent during the first seven years of repayment, 4.80 percent during the next seven years, and 4.95 percent during the final seven years.
The agreement also addresses potential delays: overdue amounts will incur default interest at 150 percent of the applicable interest rate.

The explanatory memorandum notes that in the event of payment delays exceeding six months, the loan agreement may be terminated, in which case the full amount drawn down under the credit facility becomes immediately due.
Disputes arising from the agreement are to be resolved through consultations between the parties.

The agreement on cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy was signed in Moscow on January 14 by former Minister for National Development Németh Lászlóné and Sergey Kiriyenko, head of Rosatom.
The signing was attended by Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The Hungarian Parliament approved the agreement with Russia on the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant on February 6.

The Russian–Hungarian cooperation covers the maintenance and development of the plant’s capacity, including the design, construction, commissioning, and decommissioning of two new units, each with an installed capacity of at least 1,000 megawatts, intended to replace the output of the four existing units that will be phased out in the future.
The agreement ensures that the Paks Nuclear Power Plant will remain in Hungarian state ownership.
Foreign-currency loan: over by Christmas

articles.headline: Foreign-currency loan: over by Christmas

sentences.text: There may still be issues on the expenditure side.
On Monday, Parliament approved the financial and loan agreement related to the Paks project.
LMP and other opposition parties argue that this constitutes the taking on of a €10 billion foreign-currency loan.
Between 2008 and 2009, the socialist government took out a €14 billion loan from the IMF and the European Union.
The Paks agreement, by contrast, is an investment loan.
It will result in a modernized power plant owned by the Hungarian state.
Moreover, the Hungarian state will have strong rights: it will be able to influence the share of Hungarian-owned companies involved in the project’s implementation.
A 40 percent share has been stipulated.
From this perspective, Hungarian interests are strong and clearly embedded in the agreement.
At present, no one can say with certainty whether the full loan amount will be needed.
There has not yet been a nuclear power plant investment anywhere in the world that ended up costing less than initially projected.
No one likes to disclose the final cost of such projects.
It is understandable if someone does not support nuclear power and therefore protests against it.
However, regardless of how much we favor renewable energy, the reality is that Paks cannot currently be replaced.
“They didn’t spend much time thinking this through.
The Russians came, and that was it.
This does not reduce our dependency.”
Parliament decided on the expansion in 2009, and consultations have been ongoing ever since.
In the same year, the National Assembly declared that a long-term National Energy Strategy guaranteeing the country’s energy security must be developed.
Not only the direction matters, but also the type of energy.
Until now, Hungary has been far more dependent on fossil fuels—if gas and oil prices surge, the country’s competitiveness suffers.
A diversified energy mix—from renewables through nuclear to fossil sources—is more beneficial for the country.
“Other countries also build nuclear power plants.”
“If I run a small taxi company with four identical cars that I know how to operate, repair, and understand, why would I buy a different type when expanding?
If we had opted for Korean or American technology at Paks, we would have had to retrain specialists completely and adopt unfamiliar technology.”
“The government spokesperson previously said that loan repayment would begin in ten years.
However, the press reported, based on information from the Russian side, that repayment must start this year.”
“If we do not draw down a single forint of the loan, what would we repay?
Principal repayment begins after the investment is completed.”
“How much will this increase Hungary’s public debt?”
“According to our calculations, it does not jeopardize the debt target.
The Fundamental Law also commits us to a declining debt trajectory.”
“That would require an extremely high primary surplus.”
“Over the past three years, there has always been doubt about whether our debt would decrease, yet it has declined every year.”
“In the last year, it declined particularly smoothly—almost elegantly.”
“A good player performs best on match day.
Hungary’s public debt has been steadily decreasing over the past three years, something only a few European countries can claim.”
Interview with Miklós Seszták, Minister for National Development

articles.headline: Interview with Miklós Seszták, Minister for National Development

sentences.text: Magyar Hírlap, 19 July 2014 (pp. 1, 8)
Further state acquisitions are expected
“There are key sectors of the economy where state involvement needs to be increased.
This does not mean nationalization.
The government is not nationalizing, but expanding its role in strategic sectors.

Part of this may involve acquiring certain companies on a market basis, even up to 100 percent ownership—as was the case with Antenna Hungária and Főgáz—or purchasing specific segments within a sector,” said Miklós Seszták, Minister for National Development, in an interview with our newspaper.
He also denied that there is any ban on concluding contracts within the ministry or its affiliated companies.
He noted that industrial utility price reductions are expected from next year, as “earlier implementation is not possible due to the need for preparation and legislative amendments.”
No ‘ban’ on contract conclusion at the Ministry for National Development – industrial utility price cuts realistically possible from 2015
Seszták plans for a four-year term
“The government is not nationalizing but increasing state involvement in strategic sectors.
This may include acquiring certain companies on a market basis, even entirely, or purchasing segments within a sector.
We do not intend to acquire entire systems or companies, but rather control,” Seszták emphasized.

He stated that industrial utility price reductions are expected from 2015, as “earlier implementation is not feasible due to the necessary preparatory work and legislative changes.” The head of the Ministry for National Development (NFM) also noted that the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is progressing according to plan.
– How long do you plan to serve as minister?
According to leaked reports, you may hold the position only briefly.
– Every minister and state secretary plans for a full governmental cycle.
Planning for less would be unrealistic, while planning beyond four years would be naive.
I have been appointed for this government cycle.
If that counts as long term, then I am planning for the long term.
– What new measures do you plan to introduce at the ministry?
– I come from the economic and business sector, and I aim to lead the ministry with a managerial approach.

As for new developments, consumer protection will be transferred to us from the Ministry for National Economy, as key public utility services must be handled in a unified way, and consumer protection is closely linked to this.
The ministry will also oversee the government’s sports development portfolio and the coordination of direct EU funding, although we will define the framework rather than administer the tenders.
– Isn’t this now the responsibility of the Prime Minister’s Office?
– The allocation methodology is changing.
In essence, the Prime Minister’s Office will submit proposals, while the other ministries will operate on an equal footing in handling these matters.
We will not be subordinate in decision-making.
There is one government with nine ministries; the goal is to increase efficiency.
– Companies under your supervision are currently being audited.
Why was this necessary, and what do you expect from it?
– To clarify: the audit primarily means identifying opportunities to improve efficiency and introducing a temporary moratorium on contracts not related to regular operations.
– So is there a moratorium on new contracts at companies under the ministry?
– If a company intends to conclude a contract not related to day-to-day operations, it must submit it for prior review.
There is no general ban, but in some cases it must be assessed whether a particular transaction fits our concept, financial capacity, and organizational restructuring.
– Yet many speak of a ban at the ministry.
As I said, only non-routine contracts require prior approval.
Cost efficiency, financing, and restructuring are currently at the center of attention.
– It is well known that the government aims to increase state ownership in strategic sectors such as electricity and gas.
How will this be achieved?
– This is primarily an economic rather than a legislative issue, but the objective is clear: there are key sectors where state involvement must be strengthened.
This does not mean nationalization.
The government is expanding its role in strategic sectors.
This may involve acquiring companies on a market basis—even entirely—or purchasing sectoral segments.
We do not intend to acquire entire systems or companies, but control, which is sufficient to achieve state objectives.
– A bill on regulating non-profit public utility providers is expected in autumn.
It is known that electricity and gas supply would remain profit-oriented.
Does this mean a shift from non-profit to for-profit?
– I have never said that this sector would become for-profit.
The government plans a dual structure: a nonprofit layer—for example waste management, water, and sewage services—and a “no profit” model.
The distinction may seem minimal but is economically significant.
Nonprofit means no profit elements are planned, whereas “no profit” requires minimal profit elements to ensure operation—electricity supply is a good example.
The key issue is becoming a universal service provider, while the state does not intend to purchase the network itself.
Profit is necessary to finance investments required for energy security.
In a “no profit” model, a minimal profit is generated, but it cannot be distributed as dividends and must be reinvested in energy efficiency or energy security.
– The government has been communicating for months that industrial utility price cuts will follow the household ones.
When can this be expected?
– Impact studies are currently underway.
We must determine the scope, the affected sectors, and the percentage reduction.
I can promise concrete details by the end of the year.
– So industrial price cuts are only realistic from 2015?
– Yes, earlier implementation is not feasible due to preparation and legislative requirements.
– Why are industrial utility price reductions necessary?
– Hungary’s reindustrialization requires affordable energy.
Increasing the competitiveness of domestic industry depends on reducing the cost of products and services, which requires lower energy prices.
– Which energy companies does the state intend to acquire?
– The government has expressed its intention to pursue further acquisitions.
However, it would be inappropriate for a company to learn from the press that the state intends to acquire it.
– Can utility price cuts continue indefinitely?
Will tariffs remain under political control?
– The role of the energy authority in price regulation is unquestionable and will not change.
Pricing will remain an issue of efficiency rather than politics.
There is, however, a lower limit beyond which further reductions would threaten energy security.

Results are already visible in both international comparisons and domestic indicators: Hungarian households have moved significantly away from the bottom of the European rankings in terms of energy burden.
– How do you assess the status of the Paks expansion?
– Everything is progressing according to plan.
Due to its importance, the project is supervised by a government commissioner whose work extends beyond the ministerial level.
The legal framework was established during the spring parliamentary session, and negotiations are proceeding as scheduled.
– From an energy strategy perspective, how does the ministry view Paks?
– We continue to uphold the energy mix outlined in the strategy: nuclear, coal, and renewables.
Hungary needs—and will continue to need—affordable, environmentally friendly, and secure nuclear energy.
The investment is also crucial for domestic job creation.
– The government appears to believe in the regional role of Hungary’s transport infrastructure.
How will this be developed and financed?
– Given Hungary’s central geographical position, it will always be a transit country.
We must capitalize on this advantage.
In rail transport, key opportunities lie in modernizing the Budapest–Belgrade line and constructing a freight railway bypass around the capital.
Financing commitments have been indicated by both Chinese partners and the Serbian side.
Improving transport in rural areas is equally important.
– What about popular programs such as the panel renovation scheme?
– A significant change will be the extension of the program to include family houses, making energy efficiency investments more widely accessible.
– What legislative initiatives can be expected in the autumn session?
– Compared to other ministries, we are less focused on legislative output and more on market-related activities.
However, we are working on how to handle minority stakes in majority state-owned companies that may have strategic importance.
We are also exploring ways to achieve full state ownership in key enterprises.
– The government is not nationalizing but expanding its role in strategic sectors.
– Affordable energy is essential for Hungary’s reindustrialization.
Hungarian nuclear policy could serve as an international example

articles.headline: Hungarian nuclear policy could serve as an international example

sentences.text: The achievements of Hungary’s nuclear policy send important signals to the countries participating in the General Conference that it is possible, even in the heart of Europe, to initiate reliable, efficient investments that ensure energy security, emphasized András Aradszki, State Secretary for Energy at the Ministry of National Development, on Tuesday in Vienna following the annual General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
The main topics of this year’s IAEA General Conference were nuclear safety and security.
In response to a question from MTI, the State Secretary highlighted that Hungary performed well in both areas.
The safety preparedness of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant has recently been assessed as adequate on several occasions by the IAEA.

In his address to the General Conference, the State Secretary reported on Hungary’s safe use of nuclear energy, as well as on the country’s active participation in international forums that promote both nuclear policy and scientific cooperation.
He also emphasized that Hungary remains committed to the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

Answering an MTI question, he noted that within the framework of cooperation with the IAEA, Hungary provides training for countries that are just beginning to consider nuclear energy as a source of power generation.
By supporting these countries through education and the exchange of experience, Hungary also serves important international interests, he added.
He mentioned ongoing cooperation with Vietnam, as well as significant initiatives toward Turkey and Saudi Arabia.
The State Secretary also referred to the strong scientific cooperation between the IAEA, the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences.
Hungary was the first among IAEA member states to request that the agency conduct a second evaluation of its nuclear security system.

Among the benefits of active cooperation with the IAEA, he highlighted that the return of spent fuel containing highly enriched uranium from the Hungarian Academy of Sciences’ Centre for Energy Research to Russia was made possible through international collaboration.
He stressed that Hungary’s energy security is guaranteed both by the lifetime extension of the currently operating units at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant and by the construction of new units.
The country could have lost a great deal without the Paks agreements

articles.headline: The country could have lost a great deal without the Paks agreements

sentences.text: According to Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade Péter Szijjártó, Hungary could have suffered significant losses had it not concluded the agreements related to the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.
Szijjártó made these remarks on Friday during a parliamentary session in a debate dedicated to the expansion of the plant.

He stated that the investment will substantially increase energy security, improve the country’s competitiveness, provide additional momentum to economic growth, ensure the success of energy policy, and contribute to reducing industrial utility costs.
The minister described the Paks project as the largest economic development investment of recent years, adding that the state had concluded one of the most successful agreements of recent decades.
One of these agreements, he noted, provides low-cost financing for a productive investment.
The nuclear power plant investment will generate exportable knowledge

articles.headline: The nuclear power plant investment will generate exportable knowledge

sentences.text: The capacity-maintenance investment of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant will generate exportable knowledge and experience, while also providing employment opportunities for participating companies over the next 25–30 years, said the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade on Thursday in Paks.

László Szabó, speaking at a joint business forum with Fidesz mayoral candidate György Kozmann, recalled that the capacity-maintenance project will amount to an investment of €10–12 billion, of which 40 percent—approximately €3 billion—will be accessible to Hungarian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
However, he noted that companies will require strong coordination in order to secure contracts.
Currently, around 160 companies are involved as suppliers and service providers for the nuclear power plant, but at least double that number will be needed.
“The opportunity is open to everyone; tenders related to technological preparation will already be published in October,” he stated.

He emphasized that the €3 billion is not only important for providing work to participating companies, but also for enabling them to acquire competitive, exportable knowledge and experience by meeting world-class quality standards.
He added that local SMEs are best positioned to take advantage of these opportunities.
He also noted that around 70 nuclear power plants are currently under construction worldwide, with a further 170 planned.
In Finland, for example, a plant similar to Paks is being built under an agreement between the Finnish and Russian governments, and the same standards will apply in Paks.
He added that once the new local government in Paks is established, interested SMEs will be able to quickly obtain information on participation conditions through a central coordination office.
Responding to a suggestion that involving SMEs as subcontractors could increase costs, he stressed that the role of integrators should not be underestimated.

Even if integrators have a slight cost-increasing effect, SMEs will be able to learn the required standards through cooperation and later apply independently—possibly in consortia of three to four companies—for similar projects.

articles.headline: Benedek Jávor: Go Green!

sentences.text: The Copenhagen climate summit has also drawn the attention of Hungarian public actors—usually preoccupied with provincial political skirmishes—to the crucial issue of reducing carbon dioxide emissions and replacing fossil energy sources.

While the government seeks to reaffirm its commitment to a strict new climate protection agreement, it has become entangled in scandals related to the sale of emission allowances and the use of the resulting revenues under the current system.
At the same time, relatively little is known about the energy policy plans of the largest opposition party.
However, Viktor Orbán’s visit to Russia in November provided a brief glimpse—like a flash of lightning—into the energy strategy taking shape within Fidesz.

Upon returning from Saint Petersburg, the party leader stated that extending the lifetime of the Russian-designed Paks Nuclear Power Plant and constructing new units would play a key role in reducing Hungary’s dependence on gas.

“In one of the major national economic projects aimed at reducing gas dependence, the Russians will likely be involved, even though this investment is precisely intended to lessen reliance on their gas,” he argued.

Although András Gyürk, a Fidesz MEP, recently published an article on these pages addressing energy independence in more nuanced terms, it is doubtful that his position would prevail over that of the party leader in such a strategic matter.
Orbán’s claims are difficult to reconcile.
On the one hand, he is right: Hungary’s dependence on Russian gas is unsustainable.
The high share of natural gas in Hungary’s energy mix makes the country highly vulnerable to price fluctuations and poses serious security risks.
The Ukrainian–Russian gas disputes—most recently in January 2009—have demonstrated that Russia is willing to use energy as a tool of political pressure.
Moreover, reliance on gas may hinder Hungary’s ability to meet anticipated emission reduction obligations under future climate agreements.
On the other hand, the proposed solution reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of energy policy.
Replacing gas with nuclear energy—currently also reliant on Russian fuel supply—does not address the problem.
Russian gas, primarily used for residential heating, cannot simply be substituted by electricity generated by nuclear power plants.
Electric heating is significantly more expensive than gas, even without subsidies, and would require massive technological transformation.

Converting all households to electric heating would necessitate approximately three additional “Paks-sized” power plants, at a cost of 4,000–5,000 billion forints, not including the required overhaul of the entire electricity grid.
A fraction of this amount could finance energy efficiency programs capable of halving heating costs.
In electricity generation, by contrast, replacing gas is not a key issue, nor is it feasible in the short term.
Most of Hungary’s electricity is generated not by gas, but by coal and lignite plants, as well as the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.
Gas-fired plants, due to their flexibility, play a crucial role in balancing the system—something that inflexible nuclear units cannot replace.
Although nuclear energy can effectively replace similarly inflexible coal-fired generation, it is far from certain that this is economically justified.
Numerous studies point out that building new nuclear units involves extremely high costs, both internationally and domestically, and therefore requires careful prior assessment.

In contrast, the Hungarian Parliament approved the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant in March without detailed long-term cost analyses or clarity regarding Hungary’s future emission reduction and renewable energy obligations—effectively making a blind decision.
While Gyürk’s article highlights several important issues, and presents a far more substantiated program than Orbán’s, it remains confined to a sectoral perspective.
Energy independence cannot be achieved through energy policy alone.
What is needed is a comprehensive green economic and regulatory transition.

This should include building insulation, energy efficiency and conservation measures, support for renewable energy, and a green tax system that penalizes energy and resource waste—such as introducing a carbon tax alongside reductions in labor taxes and contributions—and the phasing out of harmful subsidies that sustain inefficient systems.
It is also essential to decentralize domestic energy production and to develop, and connect to, a European smart electricity supergrid as proposed by the European Green Party.

Such a policy package must also include the gradual elimination of gas subsidies and, alongside modernization of district heating systems and the introduction of individual metering, the removal of reduced VAT rates for district heating.

The freed-up resources—supplemented by revenues from emissions trading—should be redirected into genuinely consumption- and cost-reducing investments, particularly insulation, energy-efficient technologies (such as geothermal energy), and renewable energy utilization.
Potential social consequences of rising energy prices should not be addressed through consumption-stimulating subsidies, but within the social welfare system (e.g., through housing support).
Savings from eliminating inefficient subsidies would provide adequate funding for such measures.

This green transition—a “Green New Deal”—could enable Hungary to significantly reduce CO₂ emissions, achieve genuine energy independence from uncertain external sources, and develop a green industry capable of driving the Hungarian economy in the 21st century.
Such investments would yield far greater returns and, instead of relying on Russian capital, would provide opportunities for domestic enterprises.
Népszabadság: András Schiffer on LMP, Roma integration, and Paks

articles.headline: Népszabadság: András Schiffer on LMP, Roma integration, and Paks

sentences.text: “Staying out of the trench warfare”

According to András Schiffer, lead candidate of LMP, there is no separation between a “civil self” and a “party self”: “We founded LMP to create a political actor in Hungary that does not detach itself from grassroots social organization.”
– Is it not a disadvantage in the campaign that the party has no prime ministerial candidate—no single figure embodying it?
– LMP has a national list, a lead candidate, and spokespersons.
We deliberately did not want a leader-centered party.
We are preparing for Parliament, not for government; therefore, we did not nominate a prime ministerial candidate.
– Reforming party financing is one of your key issues, but it requires a two-thirds majority.
How can politics be different if there is always someone who resists change?
– It was not only the opposition that obstructed reform.
Within MSZP, there are groups with vested interests in maintaining the current opaque system.
What is happening in Budapest is not just about Miklós Hagyó.
Nor is it simply that the two major parties could not agree.
That does not absolve Fidesz either—they derailed reform in December.
What is certain is that in our parliamentary group there will be no one opposed to change.
LMP also differs from existing parties in that our relations with others are not burdened by the conflicts that have poisoned public life over the past twenty years.
We have consciously stayed out of this “trench warfare” rooted in 20th-century grievances—and we intend to remain outside it.
We are not hostile toward those with whom we may need to negotiate on two-thirds issues.

– A presidential advisory body suggested that desegregation of Roma children should not be forced without social consensus, and that differences between schools should instead be reduced—even if this implies separate but high-quality Roma schools.
– Responsible policy requires maintaining a delicate balance.
It is unacceptable for children to be segregated into ghettos based on ethnicity or income.
That is one side of the issue.
On the other hand, attempts to enforce integration administratively, without considering the frustrations and insecurities of lower middle-class groups, can be counterproductive.
LMP would support desegregation accompanied by support mechanisms—such as psychologists and conflict-management social workers—that help create a learning-friendly environment.
Studies show that in desegregated schools, the performance of better-off children does not decline, while disadvantaged children’s performance and self-image improve.
There is no alternative to desegregation, but it requires a gradual and patient process.
– What happens to children currently in the system if there is no social consensus?
– This does not mean postponing the program.
It means designing a new “school agreement” that integrates desegregation with individualized support and a focus on learning conditions, while taking social sensitivities into account.
– Your cautious approach is also reflected in your stance on welfare policy.
While LMP opposes the “social card,” one of your candidates supported a workfare model.
– The mayor in question never supported the social card.
The regulation adopted earlier never entered into force and was intended to draw attention to the issue.
Workfare alone is not a solution.
It should have been complemented by retraining and reducing labor costs.
LMP represents a social policy that rejects punitive welfare measures.
– There was controversy over a case in which you, as a lawyer, defended a venue accused of discriminating against Roma.
– It is disgraceful to judge a lawyer based on a client’s alleged conduct.
My client was not found guilty of ethnic discrimination.
Lawyering is a profession.
If I had discovered explicit discriminatory instructions, I would have terminated the contract immediately—but no such instructions existed.
– LMP’s position on key environmental issues is not always clear.
What about Paks—should it be expanded?
– The crisis requires a transition toward sustainability and employment growth through green jobs.
We must strengthen sectors that promote sustainability, such as building renovation programs.
Reforming agricultural subsidies could help reintegrate low-skilled workers into the labor market.
This green transition would also involve tax reform, shifting the burden toward consumption and environmental impact.
– Building and operating new nuclear plants is extremely costly, beyond the environmental risks.
LMP considers it unacceptable that long-term energy decisions affecting multiple generations are made without transparency or public debate.
In the short term, nuclear energy cannot be replaced, but we believe that significant savings can be achieved through energy efficiency.
We support a diversified, decentralized energy system, with local communities increasingly becoming energy self-sufficient.
In the long term, this could partially replace both fossil and nuclear energy.
– Radar installation or environmental protection?
– I do not distinguish between a civil and a political self.
The key question is whether such installations are necessary today, not in 1995.
Given the current geopolitical context, this must be reassessed.
– LMP faces the challenge of overcoming its lack of visibility.
Why not engage more with major campaign issues such as pensions?
– Pension policy must be removed from short-term political manipulation.
With certain adjustments, we support the Swedish model.
The key is ensuring sustainability for future generations, while increasing lower pensions more significantly.
– We oppose criminalizing drug users, particularly young people.
Drug policy should focus on harm reduction and decriminalization rather than punitive approaches.
– LMP aims to attract liberal voters.
Is this a human rights issue?
– Drug policy is primarily a social policy issue, not a human rights one.
Human rights issues include police conduct during the 2006 protests or the right to housing.
LMP is committed to equal rights for all social groups, including the LGBTQ+ community, but avoids engaging in symbolic “culture wars.”
High risk – low transparency

articles.headline: High risk – low transparency

sentences.text: Hungary’s nuclear situation in light of the Japanese nuclear accident

LMP is following with concern and sympathy the efforts to manage the crisis at the Japanese nuclear power plants damaged by the earthquake, and sincerely hopes that the attempts to avert disaster will succeed.
At the same time, the events at the Fukushima and Onagawa plants draw attention to one of the most important characteristics of nuclear energy.
Although the probability of an accident is generally low, when problems occur, they involve unprecedented levels of risk.
These risks are not borne solely by political decision-makers or nuclear experts, but by all citizens.
The unresolved issue of nuclear waste disposal also raises questions of responsibility toward future generations.
Decisions on the use of nuclear energy should therefore be made with the involvement of the citizens who bear these risks, following thorough and objective information.
In Hungary, not only participation in decision-making, but also its very foundation—adequate information—has repeatedly been undermined.
Neither the lifetime extension of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, nor its planned expansion, nor the 2003 operational incident has met the requirements of transparency and public accountability.
It is indicative that several court cases are currently underway to gain access to relevant data.
In Hungary today, one must go to court to obtain information whose disclosure and public discussion would be a basic prerequisite for a fair, participatory decision-making process.
LMP insists that decisions concerning the future of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant be made through transparent and well-founded procedures.

The government should commission and publish environmental, technical, and economic impact assessments justifying the necessity of extending the plant’s lifetime or expanding it, and should commit to their open public debate.
The Japanese tragedy has once again highlighted that the use of nuclear energy is primarily a matter of safety, and only secondarily one of economic efficiency and energy policy.
It is essential to know the current technical and safety condition of each reactor at Paks, and whether it is safe and feasible to extend their operational lifetimes.
LMP insists that the review of the existing units be conducted under independent expert supervision and that the results be made public.
Committee on Sustainable Development: extraordinary session

articles.headline: Committee on Sustainable Development: extraordinary session

sentences.text: According to Benedek Jávor, Chair of the Committee, the events of recent days in Japan should prompt reflection among all those dealing with energy policy and nuclear energy.
In Hungary, seismic activity is not the primary risk factor.
The Paks Nuclear Power Plant is located along the Danube, where, as a result of climate change, much more extreme hydrological conditions can be expected than at present.

Jávor called on the government not to make any decisions regarding either the extension of the plant’s operating lifetime or the construction of new units before a thorough assessment of the risks has been carried out.
“The debate on nuclear energy cannot continue in the way it has so far.
The consequences of potential accidents are borne by society as a whole, therefore such decisions cannot be left to a narrow group of experts or solely to licensing authorities.
The public must be given the broadest possible insight and participation in these decisions.”

According to the Chair of the Committee on Sustainable Development, a broad professional and societal consultation should be initiated on Hungarian energy policy, including the future of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.
The committee approved a request for Péter Rohonyi to speak at the session on behalf of Greenpeace.

He argued that since 11 March, a new era has begun in nuclear energy, as the assumption that technological development since Chernobyl had eliminated the risk of catastrophe has proven to be unfounded.
The government should abandon the plan to expand the Paks nuclear power plant!

articles.headline: The government should abandon the plan to expand the Paks nuclear power plant!

sentences.text: LMP calls on the government to immediately abandon the plan to expand the Paks nuclear power plant and to halt all preparatory and assessment activities.
According to the green party, every minute, every forint, and every flight ticket to Moscow currently spent on preparing or even examining the expansion is wasted time and squandered public money.

It is incomprehensible that, while the Fukushima tragedy has led to the suspension and reconsideration of nuclear investments across Europe and the world, Hungary continues to push forward a mega-project that was unnecessary from the outset.
The project would consume trillions of forints in public funds, lock the Hungarian energy sector in for up to half a century, and entrench an even higher share of nuclear energy.
The Orbán government continues to press ahead with the expansion despite the fact that even prior to Fukushima there was no need for new units.

The cabinet contradicts itself by simultaneously promoting the extension of the existing reactors’ lifetimes and the construction of new ones: if the lifetime of current units is extended, there is no urgency and no need to build new capacity.
Moreover, the investment is financially unviable and exceeds the country’s economic capacity.
At the same time, inconsistent government measures in recent months have made the regulatory environment for energy projects unpredictable.

Even small power plants of around 10 MW, costing only tens of billions of forints, are currently unable to secure bank financing—let alone a 1000 MW, 3000-billion-forint expansion, which could only be realized with substantial state involvement and government guarantees.
The government should take a step back and first develop an energy strategy based on renewable energy development, improved energy efficiency, and the necessary grid infrastructure upgrades.

It is unacceptable to spend thousands of billions of forints of public money on new nuclear capacity while only 10 billion forints are allocated to energy efficiency and 26.8 billion to renewable energy under the New Széchenyi Plan.

According to LMP, nuclear energy is not the solution to the long-term energy needs of Hungary or the world; it should be phased out as soon as possible, just like depleting and climate-damaging fossil energy sources.
Singing in the Nuclear Fallout – EGP–LMP action for a nuclear-free Europe

articles.headline: Singing in the Nuclear Fallout – EGP–LMP action for a nuclear-free Europe

sentences.text: With a striking public action, the European Green Party (EGP) and Politics Can Be Different (LMP) sought to draw attention to the fact that Europe’s future must not be based on risky nuclear energy.

The Fukushima disaster has once again demonstrated that nuclear energy is too dangerous to serve as a reliable source of power for humanity; it is no coincidence that societies around the world are protesting against its use.
The European Greens have long called for the phase-out of this hazardous method of energy production, and LMP adopted the European Greens’ Charter in 2009, committing itself to a nuclear-free Europe.

Meanwhile, Hungary appears to ignore the ecological and human catastrophe unfolding in Japan, and continues to claim that the events in Fukushima do not hinder the process of expanding the Paks plant.
We wish to make it clear: Hungary does not need to expand its nuclear capacity; it is neither in the country’s interest nor financially feasible.
Far better would be to focus on clean energy production methods.
The erratic and incoherent energy strategy, along with an inadequate regulatory environment, significantly hampers the expansion of renewable energy in Hungary.

Clear political commitment and recognition of the opportunities inherent in sustainable, clean energy production—across energy policy, economic development, and employment—are necessary to replace the current centralized, inflexible, costly, and import-dependent energy system.
For the future of our country and our children, priority must be given to developing decentralized and renewable alternative energy sources.
Following the Fukushima disaster, there has been growing demand to suspend lifetime extensions of nuclear facilities and to reassess their use.

Through this action, the European Green Party and LMP express their solidarity with the victims’ families and stand for sustainable energy use that takes into account the real interests of both nature and society.
LMP turns to the courts over the Paks nuclear power plant

articles.headline: LMP turns to the courts over the Paks nuclear power plant

sentences.text: Benedek Jávor has filed a case with the Budapest Metropolitan Court to ensure that voters can finally access the documents concerning the lifetime extension and potential expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

On 28 February, the Chair of the Parliamentary Committee on Sustainable Development requested from Hungarian Electricity Works (MVM) the documentation of the so-called “Lévai project,” which determines the future of the plant.
MVM Ltd. refused to release these documents, citing business confidentiality.

According to Jávor, this refusal constitutes a violation of the law, as under data protection legislation and other relevant regulations, decisions concerning the nuclear power plant and the materials underpinning them qualify as public-interest information related to the state of the environment.
Access to such information should not be restricted to members of parliament; upon request, it must be made available to all Hungarian citizens.
Previously, the government had also failed to provide substantive answers to the LMP MP’s questions regarding transparency, when he raised the issue in Parliament before the agenda.

According to the committee chair, in light of the Fukushima disaster—classified at level 7—and the 25th anniversary of Chernobyl, the future of the plant and the use of nuclear energy constitute issues of such gravity that the government responsible for energy policy should itself initiate a broad public debate.
Instead, the authorities are withholding even basic information and attempting to make decisions without consultation.

Jávor argues that not only the safety concerns of nuclear energy and the challenges of radioactive waste management justify an open public debate, but also the allocation of several trillion forints of public funds earmarked for lifetime extension and possible expansion.
LMP calls on all stakeholders not to make decisions that fundamentally shape the country’s future behind the public’s back.
Unnecessary and rushed: the new nuclear power plant
Greenpeace condemns the plans for new Paks reactors

articles.headline: Greenpeace condemns the plans for new Paks reactors

sentences.text: Greenpeace protests against the government’s decision to classify the construction of two new nuclear reactor units at the site of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant as an investment of outstanding importance and necessity.
Péter Rohonyi, Greenpeace campaigner, stated: “Hungary does not need new units at Paks.

Nuclear electricity generation does not contribute to sustainable development, because it is inherently an unsustainable mode of energy production. (1) Instead of nuclear energy, the country should invest in renewable energy.”

Several studies, including Greenpeace’s Progressive Energy [Revolution] report, demonstrate that Hungary’s population can be provided with secure and cost-effective electricity even if the aging and dangerous Paks units are gradually phased out, no new nuclear plant is built, and most fossil-fuel-based electricity generation is also eliminated.
If Hungary makes use of its domestic potential in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and energy conservation, all of this can be achieved while creating a large number of new green jobs.
Greenpeace strongly opposes the classification of the new Paks units as a priority investment.
In the case of a nuclear project, what is most needed is caution, safeguards, and full transparency.

By contrast, designating it as a priority investment does the opposite: it allows the plans to be implemented on an accelerated schedule, in an insufficiently considered manner, and without social oversight.

Rohonyi added: “Since the Fukushima nuclear disaster, two things are more certain than ever: first, there is no such thing as safe nuclear energy; second, even a nuclear power plant that plays a major role in national electricity production can be replaced even in the short term.
The government’s nuclear plans are in sharp conflict with Hungary’s environmental interests, the basic interests of Hungarian citizens, and international trends.”
(1) As explained, among others, in an Austrian governmental expert study on nuclear energy, see pp. 243–257, for example:

“...A good deal of the lacking sustainability of nuclear industry lies in the fact that its regulatory need is met exclusively by national legislation without serious institutionalized international control or control by the European Communities, so as if the consequences of nuclear accidents would stop at national frontiers.”

“12.8 Conclusions This analysis based on several key documents beyond any doubt shows that electricity production by nuclear power plants is in clear and indisputable conflict with the principles of sustainability. ...The inevitable dilemma of the regulatory deficit of nuclear industry is topped by the fact, that roughly 60 years after the first nuclear power stations were put into operation there still is no solution for the problem of permanently repositing nuclear waste.
Its time dimension of more than one million years ultimately proves the inherent incompatibility of the production of electricity by nuclear power with the principles of sustainability.”
Renewables instead of Paks!
Even the Austrians do not understand why Hungary wants to march into a nuclear dead end

articles.headline: Even the Austrians do not understand why Hungary wants to march into a nuclear dead end

sentences.text: This afternoon, Greenpeace activists greeted Prime Minister Viktor Orbán at one stop of his visit to Vienna with banners reading “Renewables instead of Paks!” According to news reports, Austrian Chancellor Werner Faymann also expressed his incomprehension to Orbán as to why the Hungarian government insists on building a new nuclear power plant.
Márta Vetier, Program Director of Greenpeace Hungary, who was present on site, said: “In Austria, even the import of electricity generated by nuclear power plants is being banned.
Meanwhile, the Fidesz government is pushing ever more stubbornly for the construction of a new nuclear plant at Paks.

Greenpeace’s Energy [Revolution] study shows that there is no need for this dangerous project: Hungary’s secure, domestically based, and cost-effective energy supply can be ensured without Paks as well.”
Today, the Orbán government’s commitment to nuclear energy can no longer be explained on safety, energy policy, or economic grounds.
Several renewable energy technologies can already generate electricity at competitive prices if the proper market environment is in place.
“We will do everything we can to prevent the construction of the new nuclear power plant at Paks.
There is no safe nuclear energy.
These current nuclear dream-plans could shackle Hungary for decades to a bad energy system.
Nuclear power can be replaced, and therefore it must be replaced,” Vetier added.

According to Greenpeace, the most urgent task in the field of nuclear energy in Hungary is to investigate the fundamental safety issues that were left out of the stress tests, especially those arising from the type and age of the Paks plant.
The serious dangers revealed by the stress test must also be remedied urgently.
Over the coming years, the aging Paks units must be gradually shut down.
Our grandchildren will also pay for the Paks expansion
Position statement of Greenpeace Hungary on the construction of two new nuclear units at Paks

articles.headline: Position statement of Greenpeace Hungary on the construction of two new nuclear units at Paks

sentences.text: Budapest, 15 January 2014 – According to Greenpeace, the cooperation agreement announced on Tuesday between Hungary and the Russian Federation on the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant will steer Hungary’s energy policy in the wrong direction and lock it in for at least the next seventy years.
In a democratic country, such a decision is unacceptable without social debate, professional consultation, and meaningful information.

This is especially so given that a representative Medián opinion poll showed [1] that two-thirds of the Hungarian population [2] reject the expansion of Paks and would prefer the government to support renewable energy.
We call on members of Parliament not to ratify the Putin–Orbán pact on the expansion.

They should not disregard the will of voters only a few months before the elections, and above all they should not rush into such a disadvantageous deal, the burden of which even our grandchildren will still be carrying.
The Prime Minister has no right to commit the country overnight, and without substantive debate, on an issue of such enormous importance.

Among others, the Parliamentary Commissioner for Future Generations also concluded [3] that the 2011 parliamentary resolution did not authorize anyone to sign a contract for the construction of a nuclear power plant, since the decision concerned the beginning of preparations for the investment, not the investment itself.

Moreover, until last week the official government communication had spoken of an international tender, which the Prime Minister has now nullified in one stroke, since Rosatom won the deal without competition.

Viktor Orbán would commit the country to an investment of HUF 4,000–6,000 billion—around a quarter of the annual national budget—while neither the government nor the multibillion-forint Lévai Project studies [4] launched to prepare the nuclear plant have answered the most basic questions, such as why the mega-project must be launched now, or how electricity that costs twice the current market price can be called cheap.
For a long time we have heard the government’s mantra: expanding the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is unavoidable and will bring Hungary clean, cheap electricity.
Decision-makers seem not to recognize any other energy sources and have not meaningfully examined alternatives.

Greenpeace is firmly convinced, on professional grounds, that building a new nuclear power plant is unnecessary and far too expensive; and because of the lack of social consultation and the concealment of essential information, it is also not credible and unacceptable.
Do not let them pack away our future!

articles.headline: Do not let them pack away our future!

sentences.text: Open letter to Members of Parliament and appeal to all Hungarian citizens

Budapest, 23 January 2014 – Today, Energiaklub, Greenpeace Hungary, the Clean Air Action Group, Friends of the Earth Hungary, the organizers of the Paks vobiscum? conference, and Védegylet addressed an open letter to Hungarian MPs demanding that they withhold their consent to the intergovernmental agreement on the construction of Paks 2.
The parliamentary vote on the agreement may take place very soon, possibly as early as the first week of February.
Therefore, the organizations are also calling on every person who thinks responsibly about the future.

They ask everyone who agrees that a decision of this magnitude must not be made without broad social consultation to join the cause at the website www.pakskontroll.hu and, with the click of a button, send the open letter to Hungarian MPs.
On 13 January, the Hungarian government committed the country to the expansion of Paks, to a 30-year loan, and to an investment of at least HUF 4,000 billion.
This decision was taken unlawfully, without proper foundation, and in total secrecy.
Since 2009, convincing public evidence has never once been presented showing that this is the best solution for Hungary.
The agreement will enter into force if Parliament votes in favor of it in early February.
MPs have a duty to express the will of their voters through their vote.

That is why the organizations behind the open letter ask everyone to use the www.pakskontroll.hu website to inform MPs that they do not agree with the way the process has been conducted and that they want to participate in the decision on Paks 2.
MPs bear personal responsibility to their voters not to allow this agreement to enter into force.
We have only two weeks left until the vote; there is no time to lose.
The country’s independence, our future security, and our prosperity now depend on the representatives’ decision.
We can still prevent the Paks pact

articles.headline: We can still prevent the Paks pact

sentences.text: Budapest, 30 January 2014 – This morning, Greenpeace activists transformed Clark Ádám Square in Budapest into a giant nuclear symbol.
With this striking action, they drew attention to the fact that the process of expanding Paks—unacceptable from both environmental and economic perspectives—must be stopped.
The government may submit the matter to Parliament for approval as early as next week.
Every single MP must feel the personal responsibility of the decision they make in this matter, since there is a better solution to meeting electricity demand than Paks 2.
As early as 2011, Greenpeace published its Energy [Revolution] report [1], showing that the gradual phase-out of nuclear energy is a realistic alternative.
Hungary’s future energy needs can be met by a decentralized system based largely on domestic renewable resources by 2050 at the latest.
If the Energy [Revolution] scenario is implemented, in the 2030s we could leave behind the safety and environmental risks associated with an operating nuclear power plant, as well as fuel dependency.
Numerous analyses published since the signing of the Paks pact also show that electricity generated by a new nuclear power plant cannot be competitive at current prices. [2]

Greenpeace calls on everyone who disagrees with this irresponsible and ill-prepared decision to join the civil protest to be held in Budapest on Saturday, 1 February, at 3:30 p.m. at József Nádor Square.
Let us show MPs that we do not agree with them making such a far-reaching decision in our name without examining alternatives and counterarguments.
Greenpeace firmly calls on Members of Parliament not to vote for the Paks expansion, but to give the country time to examine the real alternatives.
This decision must not be made now and must not be made in this way.
Energy dependence or freedom?

articles.headline: Energy dependence or freedom?

sentences.text: Budapest, 3 February 2014 – This morning, Greenpeace activists protested against Paks 2 with banners at one of the symbols of Hungary’s independence, the Liberty Statue in Budapest.
With this, they sent a message to Members of Parliament.
Greenpeace once again strongly urges MPs not to support the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant with their votes.
The bill submitted at breakneck speed would trap the country in energy dependence for another 60–70 years.
Greenpeace also demands the publication of the analyses, studies, and background materials related to the expansion.
On the very day the bill was submitted, news also emerged that documents relating to the preparation of the intergovernmental agreement had been classified for ten years.
Greenpeace points out that without these documents, the claim that the plant has no alternative cannot be substantiated, and nothing supports the assertion that this is the best deal for Hungary.
History has shown that decisions made without broad social consensus do not endure for long.

According to Greenpeace analysts, there would be no market for the surplus electricity generated during the simultaneous operation of Paks 1 and Paks 2. [1] Based on the official energy policy documents and statements of neighboring countries, it appears that no one will need additional electricity by 2030.
The neighboring countries are already either electricity exporters, do not accept nuclear energy, or—like Hungary—are developing capacity in hopes of exporting.
This is also true of Germany, which in 2012 exported 22.8 TWh of electricity as a net exporter despite having shut down eight nuclear power plants since the Fukushima disaster in 2011.
For Hungary, there are only better solutions than nuclear energy, which carries enormous environmental, safety, and economic risks.
MPs must not forget even for a moment that they are voting with the long-term interests of their constituents in mind.
In the case of a 60–70-year investment, four-year cycles and party loyalties must be forgotten.
Every single representative bears personal responsibility not to support a classified investment that causes energy dependence and will never pay for itself economically.
Expanding the nuclear power plant would place the country on such a narrow energy and economic path that energy efficiency and renewables could only play a severely subordinate role.
The decision has been made; the debate starts now

articles.headline: The decision has been made; the debate starts now

sentences.text: Budapest, 6 February 2014 – Today, the National Assembly enacted the law on the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant by roll-call vote.
This new law gives the green light, for the next 60–70 years, to an outdated, continuously dangerous, expensive, and inflexible energy source.
MPs missed the historic opportunity for a well-founded decision to be made after substantive debate, and for Hungary to embark already now on the path toward energy independence.
Representatives voted for the bill despite the fact that experts, civil society organizations—including Greenpeace—and citizens had all entered the debate with serious counterarguments.
Since Prime Minister Viktor Orbán returned from Moscow with the pact, virtually only dissenting opinions from independent sources have been heard.
On the morning of the vote, Greenpeace handed MPs several expert materials [1] at the entrance to Parliament showing that Paks 2 does indeed have alternatives.
The electricity that the new nuclear units would generate can be produced from renewable sources, and more cheaply than under the current giant investment.
“Every MP who voted for the Paks pact bears personal responsibility to the electorate for the long-term consequences of this decision.
Greenpeace will continue working, using every available legal and social means, to stop this investment.
The sooner we succeed, the less we will spend on a concrete sarcophagus that will never produce anything,” said Zsolt Szegfalvi, head of Greenpeace.

Following Parliament’s decision, Greenpeace, together with the civil coalition opposing the Paks pact, turned to President János Áder and asked him, in the interest of Hungarian citizens and future generations, not to sign the Paks law.
240 Greenpeace activists warn: Europe has entered a new danger zone

articles.headline: 240 Greenpeace activists warn: Europe has entered a new danger zone

sentences.text: Budapest, 5 March 2014 – Today, 240 Greenpeace activists across Europe, including 11 from Hungary, are drawing attention to the dangers of nuclear power generation.
In Hungary, this message is especially timely because of the planned expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

In light of the serious environmental risks and the events that have unfolded in our immediate neighborhood in recent months, Greenpeace calls on the Hungarian government to suspend and review the contract that would entrust the construction of two new reactor units at Paks to the giant corporation Rosatom.
The planned new nuclear plant—unnecessary in any case—would plunge Hungary into even deeper energy dependence and an even more vulnerable economic position than at present.
“We still have a chance to steer Hungary away from the path of nuclear energy production, which carries serious environmental dangers.
Greenpeace’s aim is to put the country on a new path based on renewable energy sources and energy efficiency—an alternative that is already realistic today.
All that is missing is the political will,” said Brigitta Bozsó, Greenpeace Hungary campaigner.
Today, in connection with the actions, Greenpeace also published a new report entitled Entering a New Danger Zone: Lifetime Extension of Aging Nuclear Power Plants.
The study, prepared by independent European experts, explores the technical dangers associated with aging, and analyzes the economic and insurance risks.
It also warns that extending the operating life of nuclear reactors marks the beginning of a new, more dangerous era in Europe.
The average age of nuclear power plants is already 29 years. (At Paks, Unit 1 began operating on 28 December 1982.)

Alongside the report, Greenpeace also launched a continuously updated website in English at www.out-of-age.eu, where citizens can inform themselves and express their view that they do not want to live in an expanded danger zone instead of choosing real, clean, and safe solutions.
Greenpeace activists highlight the dangers of nuclear energy

articles.headline: Greenpeace activists highlight the dangers of nuclear energy

sentences.text: Budapest, 11 March 2014 – On the third anniversary of the Fukushima nuclear disaster, Greenpeace activists projected the message “Stop Paks 2” and a giant image of “The Scream” onto the side of the MPs’ Office Building in Budapest.

Through this, the activists sought to highlight the dangers of nuclear energy and simultaneously call on current and future Members of Parliament not to vote for the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.
The serious nuclear accident that occurred at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant in 2011 has, even after three years, created a disaster situation in Japan that remains unresolved.
More than 100,000 people still live far from their homes, with no clear prospects.
As a result, despair and distrust toward the authorities continue to grow.

One-third of families are separated from their children, 35% are forced to live on roughly half their former income, and the majority are still waiting in temporary accommodation for the situation to improve.
Those affected are struggling to process the mental and physical trauma: a recent survey showed that 37% suffer from sleep disorders.
We must not forget that a nuclear disaster can happen at any time.
Nowhere are we protected against the combination of human error and natural events.
Cleaning up the Fukushima plant site and surrounding areas could take as long as 50–60 years, at an estimated cost of $250–500 billion.
The work carried out over the past three years has been accompanied by repeated mistakes, cover-ups, leaks, and malfunctions.
It appears that TEPCO, the company operating the plant, is unable to keep the situation under control.
There are still places within the evacuation zone where background radiation is 20–50 times the permitted limit.
The people living in Fukushima Prefecture completely reject nuclear energy after the disaster.

A plan has now been developed showing how the region’s two million inhabitants could be supplied entirely from renewable energy sources. [1] Japanese society likewise favors a nuclear phase-out: 76% would eliminate nuclear energy from the energy supply, 53% gradually and 23% immediately. [2]

“Hungary also has the possibility to supply the population and the economy with the energy they need without nuclear power; we do not have to live with the risks and pollution that come with it,” said Brigitta Bozsó, Greenpeace climate and energy campaigner.
“Greenpeace’s Energy [Revolution] report [3] also points to this path, and a scenario prepared for the National Energy Strategy likewise exists that does not assume the expansion of the plant.
In Europe, too, a number of countries—largely under the influence of the Fukushima disaster—have said no to nuclear energy.
These include Germany, Italy, Austria, and Denmark, while Switzerland and Spain will not build any new nuclear plants either.
It is time for Hungary as well to embark on the path of sustainable energy management and move away from highly dangerous and costly nuclear energy.
It is the personal responsibility and duty of MPs to make this decision.
Greenpeace therefore once again strongly calls on them not to support the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.”
Greenpeace demands the publication of the facts in the Paks 2 case

articles.headline: Greenpeace demands the publication of the facts in the Paks 2 case

sentences.text: Budapest, 2 April 2014 – Yesterday, the Hungarian public once again learned from the Russian press that the Hungarian government had secretly signed a €10 billion loan agreement with Russia regarding the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, without parliamentary authorization.
