Greenpeace Hungary demands that the government immediately publish the full text of the loan agreement and the details of the Russian–Hungarian deal, still before the elections.
We call on the Hungarian government to dispel the fog surrounding the Paks 2 contract:
provide information on whether a parliamentary vote is necessary for the contract to enter into force, or whether Parliament is merely to be informed;
clarify whether the contract entered into force immediately upon signature.

At a time when the European Union, in connection with the Ukrainian crisis, is doing everything it can to minimize dependence on Russian energy, the Hungarian government is doing everything it can to tie us ever more tightly to Russia.
Hungary’s current dependence on imported oil and gas is close to 80%; with the signed Paks agreement, dependence in electricity generation could approach 80% in the 2030s.
This would be unprecedented in Europe.

The goal of Greenpeace Hungary is that, instead of relying on outdated, continuously dangerous, expensive, and inflexible energy sources, Hungary should move as soon as possible onto the path of real energy independence: increasing energy efficiency and making use of renewable energy sources.

On Thursday, 3 April 2014, at 11:30 a.m., Greenpeace activists will stage a visual protest at Batthyány Square (on the Danube-side bicycle path in the direction of Margit Bridge) against Hungary’s growing energy dependence.
Are we really heading in the right direction?

articles.headline: Are we really heading in the right direction?

sentences.text: Budapest, 3 April 2014 – Greenpeace activists today staged a striking protest against Hungary’s increasing energy vulnerability.
Hungary’s current oil and gas dependence is close to 80%, and with the signed Paks agreement, dependence in electricity generation could likewise approach 80% in the 2030s.
The upcoming elections are also about stopping the Paks investment, since the government—bypassing both Parliament and the public—has rushed into a loan agreement with the Russian state.
While the European Union is doing everything it can, in light of the Ukrainian crisis, to reduce dependence on Russia, the Hungarian government is tying us ever more tightly to Russia.
We learned from the Russian press that the government has signed the intergovernmental loan agreement that would make possible the expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.
“This is today Hungary’s most important environmental and economic issue, and in fact the worst investment of the century.
The government made its decision hastily, without informing the public or Parliament, even though very serious criticisms have been raised and real alternatives do exist.
Nuclear energy is the past; renewable energy is the future,” said Brigitta Bozsó, Greenpeace Hungary campaigner.

There is enormous potential in energy conservation and efficiency [1], and renewables are already price-competitive. [2] Instead of near-total dependence, we could choose energy independence [3], supplying the country with 75% clean energy.
What is at stake in Sunday’s election is also whether voters will give their blessing to the government’s unexplained and last-century energy policy.
“Over the past four years, nothing has happened in the field of renewable energy beyond promises, and that represents a serious disadvantage for Hungary,” Bozsó added.
Because of the Ukrainian crisis, the EU has raised the prospect of serious sanctions, and several countries have reviewed their economic ties with Russia.
The Czech Republic, Finland, Sweden, and the United Kingdom are all stepping back from cooperation with Rosatom.
It seems Hungary is the only country deepening its dependence on Russia without reservation.
“Are we really heading in the right direction?” Greenpeace asks rhetorically.
Background information to our press release entitled “80% energy dependence?!”
Is Hungary going in the right direction?

articles.headline: Is Hungary going in the right direction?

sentences.text: Around 80% of Hungary’s gas supply depends on Russia, and 78% of its oil also comes from there.
The Paks Nuclear Power Plant currently provides roughly 45% of the country’s electricity generation.
If nuclear capacity is doubled, this share could rise to as much as 80% during the period when all six units operate together. [1]
The question is what we would do with so much surplus nuclear electricity at all.
Based on the official energy policy documents of neighboring countries, it seems that no one will need extra electricity by 2030.
Neighboring countries are either already electricity exporters, do not accept nuclear energy, or—like Hungary—are developing capacity in hopes of exporting.
This is also true of Germany, which in 2012 exported 22.8 TWh of electricity as a net exporter despite shutting down eight nuclear power plants after the Fukushima disaster in 2011.
Following the occupation of Crimea, the European Union is doing everything it can to reduce dependence on Russian energy.

In light of the obvious security risks, the Czech Republic, Finland [2], the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Sweden [3], Germany [4], and the EU are rethinking agreements to be concluded with the Russian state and Russian companies.

Meanwhile, the Hungarian–Russian agreement on the Paks expansion continues to move forward uninterrupted. [5] Prime Minister Viktor Orbán reacted to the international realignment by stating that Hungary does not support raising restrictions against Russia to a higher level. [6] We are slowly being left alone in the region with this approach, increasingly committing Hungary to a country that keeps its partners on a short leash through actual military occupation and the weaponization of energy supply.

As early as the beginning of March, the Czech defense minister stated that, because of the military occupation of Crimea, he could not imagine that a Russian company should win the tender for the expansion of the Temelín nuclear power plant. [7] Last week, news also came from the United Kingdom that British authorities are reviewing earlier cooperation with the Russian state-owned nuclear company Rosatom. [8]
If EU economic sanctions come into effect, they could severely affect Russia’s energy industry.

Sergey Kiriyenko, President of Rosatom, is also aware of this: in Moscow, he stated that the company’s foreign contracts could fall under the sanctions regime. [9] Although both Kiriyenko and Viktor Orbán, signatories of the Paks agreement, are officially optimistic about the nuclear investment, it is becoming increasingly clear that Europe is turning away from Russian investments and, instead of accepting further dependence, is seeking an exit by sourcing alternative energy supplies.

Before the next summit of heads of state, the European Commission is preparing an analysis on establishing EU energy independence, in which reducing dependence on Russian gas and oil imports will play a central role.
Sanctions could, of course, also provoke retaliatory measures from Russia.
At present, about a quarter of Europe’s gas and oil consumption comes from Russia, and around half of gas imports to the EU flow through Ukraine.

It would not be unprecedented for Moscow to turn off the gas tap: in both 2006 and 2009, Russia suspended gas deliveries to Ukraine as a result of economic disputes. [10] From April this year, industrial consumers in Ukraine will pay 29% more for gas, and public institutions 64% more, because Moscow has raised prices. [11]
Hungary would also be sensitive to any drying up of foreign loans.
According to international rating agencies, Russia is on the brink of a downgrade. [12]
What is the real solution?
Instead of 80% dependence, we could choose a clean and secure energy supply system.

According to Greenpeace’s Progressive Energy [Revolution] scenario, by 2040 more than 50% of primary energy demand could be covered by domestic renewable sources, while by 2050 this share could rise to 75%.
In addition to Greenpeace’s Energy [Revolution] report, many other calculations show that an energy supply based on efficiency and renewables is the solution.
It is not more expensive; indeed—unlike the Paks investment—it is an investment that clearly pays off.

Electricity from Paks will not be cheap: even under the most optimistic calculations, it would cost more than €100/MWh, or around HUF 31/kWh. [13] The mandatory feed-in tariff for electricity generated from solar and wind power in Hungary is currently between HUF 22 and 36/kWh during peak periods. [14] And that is not even mentioning other benefits: renewables create far more jobs than nuclear energy.
In Germany, for example, the renewable energy sector supports twice as many jobs as all other segments of the energy sector combined. [15]

There is also enormous potential in efficiency: according to a recent calculation, over 25 years less than half the cost of Paks 2 would be enough to halve heating costs in Hungary’s building stock. [16] The state would continuously recover the entire amount invested from VAT on materials and labor, payroll contributions, and secondary consumption.
Other calculations compare nuclear costs with renewables.

These clearly show that wind power, for example, is already competitive with the price of Paks. [17, 18] And finally one more fact: in the first quarter of this year, because of increased renewable generation, wholesale electricity prices in Spain almost halved, from €52/MWh to €26/MWh. [19]

Foreign Minister János Martonyi recently stated that the Hungarian economy is one of the most exposed to sanctions against Russia, primarily because of the high share of gas supply. [20] It follows clearly from the above that the government should not make Hungary almost totally dependent on Russian energy sources and technologies while domestic clean energy sources remain neglected.
Would the state pay for the nuclear power plant?
Open letter to Minister of Finance Péter Oszkó and Minister of Transport, Communications and Energy Péter Hónig

articles.headline: Open letter to Minister of Finance Péter Oszkó and Minister of Transport, Communications and Energy Péter Hónig

sentences.text: Given that the cost of the planned new reactor unit(s) at Paks would amount to at least HUF 2,000 billion, it is by no means irrelevant from which sources the investor, the state-owned MVM Ltd., intends to raise this sum.
European Union rules on state aid [1] prohibit state involvement in energy investments.
International examples [2] also clearly demonstrate that market-based financing of nuclear power plants is currently unfeasible due to the ongoing credit crisis.

In light of these facts, it is unacceptable that in a matter which will significantly affect the country’s financial situation in the long term, a company is making statements [3] and pre-empting decisions, while the relevant ministries have not taken a position.
Therefore, we expect you, as the ministers responsible for state assets and energy affairs, to clarify the following questions:

How can any meaningful decision be made regarding the financing of a multi-thousand-billion forint project when key details (the exact size [4], number, and type of reactors, the basis of cost estimates, additional associated costs, etc.) remain unclear?

How do you interpret the statement made on 14 February by János Süli, CEO of Paks Nuclear Power Plant Ltd. [5], according to which “state participation should be at least fifty plus one percent, but the goal is seventy-five percent state ownership”?
On what authorization can the Board of Directors of MVM Ltd. decide on the financing of the unit(s)?
What are the limits of decision-making authority for the companies involved (MVM Ltd., Paks Nuclear Power Plant Ltd.)?

Given that, despite our request to MVM Ltd., we have not received information on the details of the preparatory Teller and Lévai projects, we trust that you will clarify these issues, which are of outstanding importance for the Hungarian economy, consumers, and taxpayers alike.
Secret expansion at Paks – who is entitled to the details?

articles.headline: Secret expansion at Paks – who is entitled to the details?

sentences.text: While the nuclear sector has long promised open and transparent communication to a public sensitive to nuclear issues, it is unwilling to account publicly for the costs of the project preparing the planned expansion of Paks.
According to Energiaklub, this constitutes information of public interest, and therefore it has chosen to pursue legal action to gain access to the data.
Energiaklub is suing the Paks Nuclear Power Plant because it refused to disclose data from the so-called Teller Project concerning the plant’s expansion.

Energiaklub requested specific data from the Teller Project conducted prior to the 2009 parliamentary decision—primarily information on project costs and contracts concluded within the project—arguing that these qualify as public interest information.

The power plant refused to provide the requested information, claiming that “Paks Nuclear Power Plant Ltd. is not owned by the Hungarian State,” and therefore is not subject to data protection and public finance regulations.
Energiaklub fundamentally maintains that data related to the planned expansion should be public.
As this is a legal dispute, clarification now rests with the courts.
Within its Energy Control Program, Energiaklub systematically requests data on energy-related matters.
Since January 2009, it has sought information and documents in numerous cases from authorities, state bodies, and companies.
In some cases, the requested data were not provided, prompting appeals to the Data Protection Commissioner or legal action.
Ongoing cases include contracts related to strategic gas storage, data on subsidies for cogeneration plants, and MVM’s contracts with electricity producers.
Energiaklub’s legal representation in these cases is provided by the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union (TASZ).
Secret expansion at Paks (press release)

articles.headline: Secret expansion at Paks (press release)

sentences.text: How much would the planned expansion of the Paks nuclear reactor cost the Hungarian state?
And how much did the preparatory Teller Project cost?
These questions remain unanswered.
Even the latter appears to be classified.
Energiaklub considers this information to be of public interest and has therefore initiated legal proceedings against the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.
Further details are available in the attached press release or from András Perger, project leader for conventional energy carriers at Energiaklub.
Paks agreements will be made public

articles.headline: Paks agreements will be made public

sentences.text: In its ruling on Wednesday, the Tolna County Court ordered Paks Nuclear Power Plant Ltd. to disclose data from the Teller Project underpinning the planned expansion.
The defendant must publish documents on the project’s total cost and contracts concluded within 15 days.
The background is that in 2007, Paks Nuclear Power Plant and its owner, MVM Ltd., launched the Teller Project to prepare for expansion.
Given expert estimates placing the cost at HUF 2,000–3,000 billion, Energiaklub argued that the process must be transparent from the outset.
After the plant refused to provide the requested financial data and contracts, Energiaklub initiated legal proceedings.
The final ruling established that the plant, as a state-owned entity via MVM, manages public assets and must allow public scrutiny.
The Paks decision was unfounded

articles.headline: The Paks decision was unfounded

sentences.text: According to a statement published by Sándor Fülöp, Parliamentary Commissioner for Future Generations, the need for a new nuclear power plant was not examined, and the public was not informed about the preparatory process.

The statement largely confirmed Energiaklub’s concerns: no impact assessments or strategic environmental assessments were conducted, the wording of the parliamentary resolution was unclear, and it failed to specify the number of reactors or time limits.
The Commissioner emphasized that public participation must be ensured at every stage to properly assess risks.
Paks contracts made public

articles.headline: Paks contracts made public

sentences.text: Energiaklub obtained contracts from the Teller Project following a court ruling.
However, the total project cost was still not disclosed.
Based on available data, approximately HUF 470 million was spent on contracts, including project management, communication, legal consultancy, and technical analyses.
Some details were redacted, and attachments were missing; further inquiries were submitted.
Planned Paks expansion still unclear

articles.headline: Planned Paks expansion still unclear

sentences.text: Despite court rulings, important data in the released documents remain redacted or missing.
Energiaklub has requested full disclosure, including underlying studies.
The importance of transparency is underscored by a criminal investigation into one contract allegedly causing significant financial damage.
Paks contracts without redactions

articles.headline: Paks contracts without redactions

sentences.text: Following further requests, the plant released the contracts in full.
Previously redacted sections included strategies on public acceptance and radioactive waste management.
Energiaklub also requested the underlying studies.
All Paks data must be public – according to the court

articles.headline: All Paks data must be public – according to the court

sentences.text: The Budapest Court ordered MVM Ltd. to disclose data from the Lévai Project.
Required disclosures include total costs, timelines, results, participating entities, and contracts.
The ruling reaffirmed that such data are of public interest, though technical details may be redacted.
“Nuclear energy is a dying technology” – Energiaklub on Paks II

articles.headline: “Nuclear energy is a dying technology” – Energiaklub on Paks II

sentences.text: Energiaklub expert András Perger expressed skepticism about building two new reactors within a €10 billion budget, stating that such a project would not be taken seriously internationally and is unaffordable domestically.
He argued that nuclear power is becoming economically uncompetitive compared to renewables, citing cost overruns in Finland and France, financing difficulties, and declining renewable energy costs.
Financing remains the key barrier;
Demand projections are uncertain and possibly overstated;
Nuclear capacity could lead to overproduction;
Renewable technologies are becoming faster and cheaper to deploy.
He concluded that committing to nuclear energy now could lock Hungary into an expensive and outdated system for decades, while more flexible and cost-effective alternatives are available.
